newsitem.title: INDIA: Foreign investment in India power sector seen slow.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investment in India power sector seen slow.

text.p: India's decision to open the power transmission sector to private enterprise will attract huge amounts of domestic investment but foreign participation may be delayed, an Indian minister said on Wednesday.

"Foreign investment probably may take time, but I think a lot of domestic investment will come not only from the corporate sector but also from the cooperative sector," Planning Minister Yogendra Alagh told Reuters.
He gave no reasons for the anticipated delay.
On Tuesday, the Indian cabinet approved a proposal to allow private and foreign investment in electricity transmission.
India, which began to tear down its socialist protectionist barriers under an economic reform programme that began in 1991, is finding the pace of reforms has slowed because of a shortage of power.

It will need to boost its power generating capacity from 80,000 MW annually to 148,000 MW by 2001, the power ministry has estimated. The bulk of this investment will have to come from private enterprise.
Alagh was optimistic that much of this could be met from within the country.
"For domestic private investment, the sky is the limit," Alagh said, speaking to Reuters on the sidelines of an energy conference in the Indian capital.
But he had no precise estimate of the investment expected.
The gap between energy supply and demand is expected to be between eight and nine percent during the ninth five year plan (1992-2002), Alagh said.
"We will have an energy deficit of 8-9 percent," he said. "Whenever there is a slack in private investment the state will have to step in."
Alagh said nuclear power could emerge as a preferred option to the environmental costs and lengthy gestation period for hydro-power plants, especially when far away from coal reserves.
"At locations which are far removed from coal reserve areas, nuclear power can be a solid economic option," Alagh said.
